concept.name: Async/Await & Deadlock Avoidance

relationships.description: Connects Async/Await & Deadlock Avoidance to python concurrency nogil in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Async/await turns non-blocking I/O into sequential-looking state machines, but mixing synchronous blocking calls, single-threaded event loops, or non-async-aware locks can freeze an entire runtime.
spark.keyTakeaway: Never block an async worker thread waiting on a task that needs that same thread or executor to finish—use non-blocking awaits, async-aware locks, or dedicated blocking pools.

concept.whyItMatters: Modern services run thousands of concurrent requests on a small pool of OS threads (for example, 8–16 Tokio or Node/libuv workers, or a single Python asyncio loop). One `.Result`, `future.get()`, or `time.sleep()` inside an async path stalls the carrier thread, starving unrelated coroutines and causing cascading p99 latency spikes or complete liveness failure.
whenToUse: High-concurrency I/O-bound workloads (HTTP/gRPC gateways, database clients, fan-out aggregators) where threads spend >90% of time waiting on sockets.
Structured concurrency trees where parent tasks spawn bounded child tasks and cancel them cleanly on timeout or error.
Single-threaded UI or event-loop runtimes (Python asyncio, JavaScript, .NET UI threads) needing responsive non-blocking orchestration.
whenNotToUse: CPU-bound tight loops (video encoding, cryptographic hashing, ML inference) without offloading to a dedicated thread or process pool.
Simple synchronous batch scripts or CLI tools where blocking OS threads or Java Virtual Threads is simpler and avoids function-coloring overhead.
Low-level kernel or lock-free ring-buffer paths where state-machine heap allocations and poll overhead exceed raw thread costs.
keyPoints: Blocking-on-async deadlock: calling `.Result` / `.Wait()` (C#), `CompletableFuture.get()` (Java), or `loop.run_until_complete()` (Python) on a thread that owns the continuation context or exhausts a fixed thread pool.
SynchronizationContext / executor capture: by default, `await` resumes on the captured context; if that context's single thread is blocked waiting for the task, neither can proceed.

Sync mutex across `.await` points: holding a standard OS `std::sync::Mutex` or `threading.Lock` while yielding lets another task on the same thread try to acquire the lock, causing immediate self-deadlock.
Thread-pool starvation: even without a single-threaded context, blocking all N workers in a bounded pool (e.g., `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()`) prevents completion callbacks from ever being scheduled.

Cancellation & lock-order inversion: acquiring two async locks in opposite orders (`Lock A -> await -> Lock B` vs `Lock B -> await -> Lock A`) deadlocks just like OS threads, and dropping a future mid-protocol can leave state corrupt.

examples.title: UI / Single-Thread Context Capture Deadlock
examples.scenario: A C# ASP.NET (pre-Core) or desktop handler on a single-threaded `SynchronizationContext` calls `FetchUserAsync().Result` while `FetchUserAsync` awaits an HTTP call without `ConfigureAwait(false)`.
examples.outcome: The HTTP call finishes on an I/O thread, but its continuation is posted back to the captured `SynchronizationContext`, which is permanently blocked inside `.Result`. Both threads wait forever.

examples.title: Bounded Executor Starvation in Java CompletableFuture
examples.scenario: An 8-core service uses `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` (7 worker threads) for `supplyAsync()` tasks that synchronously call `.join()` on nested `supplyAsync()` calls under 50 concurrent requests.
examples.outcome: All 7 pool threads block inside `.join()` waiting for child tasks queued in the same pool. With zero free workers to run the children, throughput drops to 0 req/s.

tradeOffs.factor: Sync Mutex vs Async Mutex (e.g., tokio::sync::Mutex)
tradeOffs.pro: OS/sync mutexes have ~15–25 ns uncontended overhead and zero heap/waker bookkeeping when never held across `.await`.
tradeOffs.con: Holding a sync mutex across `.await` risks thread-pool starvation and single-thread self-deadlock; async mutexes add waker overhead but yield cleanly.

tradeOffs.factor: ConfigureAwait(false) / Explicit Executors vs Context Capture
tradeOffs.pro: Disabling context capture eliminates single-thread continuation deadlocks and avoids cross-thread queue hops (~1–5 µs saved per await).
tradeOffs.con: Downstream code after `await` loses thread-local/UI context and must explicitly marshal back when mutating UI or thread-confined state.

tradeOffs.factor: Async/Await State Machines vs OS/Virtual Threads
tradeOffs.pro: Async tasks use ~200–500 bytes per suspended future vs ~1 MB default OS thread stack, enabling 100k+ concurrent connections.
tradeOffs.con: Requires explicit async function coloring and strict discipline against accidental blocking calls in third-party libraries.

failureModes.name: Sync-over-Async Context Deadlock
failureModes.description: A caller blocks a single-threaded event loop or SynchronizationContext waiting for a future whose continuation requires that same loop.
failureModes.mitigation: Propagate `async`/`await` all the way to the entry point (`async all the way`), or use `ConfigureAwait(false)` in library code.

failureModes.name: Executor Pool Exhaustion
failureModes.description: Parent tasks block all threads in a fixed-size pool waiting on child tasks submitted to the exact same pool.
failureModes.mitigation: Offload blocking calls to a dedicated unbounded/separate blocking pool (`tokio::task::spawn_blocking`, `asyncio.to_thread`, or custom `ExecutorService`) and use non-blocking `thenCompose`.

failureModes.name: Mutex Held Across Yield Point
failureModes.description: Task A acquires a non-async lock, hits `.await`, and suspends; Task B runs on the same worker thread and blocks trying to acquire the same lock.
failureModes.mitigation: Scope sync locks tightly inside synchronous blocks so guards drop before `.await`, or use an async-aware lock (`asyncio.Lock`, `tokio::sync::Mutex`).

failureModes.name: Async Lock-Order Inversion
failureModes.description: Two concurrent coroutines acquire async locks or semaphores in opposite orders (`A then B` vs `B then A`) with an `.await` between acquisitions.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce a strict global lock acquisition hierarchy, acquire multiple locks atomically, or wrap acquisitions with bounded timeouts.

commonMistakes: Calling `time.sleep()`, `requests.get()`, or `psycopg2` inside a Python `async def` coroutine instead of `asyncio.sleep()`, `httpx.AsyncClient`, or `asyncpg`.
Using `.Result` or `.get()` inside async callbacks as a quick bridge to synchronous interfaces.
Holding a `threading.Lock` or `std::sync::Mutex` guard across an `await` expression.
Forgetting to bound concurrency with a semaphore when fanning out thousands of `asyncio.gather` / `Promise.all` tasks, exhausting connection pools and causing lock contention.
Ignoring `CancelledError` / `AbortSignal` cleanup, leaving acquired locks or database transactions open when a parent timeout fires.

sections.content:
## The idea

Compilers transform every `async` function into a cooperative state machine: each `await` is a suspension point where the function saves its local variables into a heap- or stack-allocated frame and returns control to an executor. Unlike preemptive OS threads, an executor only switches tasks at explicit `await` boundaries. Whenever code executes a synchronous blocking operation—such as `.Result`, `Thread.sleep()`, or acquiring an OS mutex—it hijacks the underlying carrier thread. If the awaited work needs that same carrier thread (or a thread from the same exhausted pool) to execute its continuation, the system enters a circular wait with zero forward progress.

## Concrete walkthrough

Consider a Python `asyncio` service with a single event-loop thread handling `/checkout`:

1. Request 1 enters `async def checkout()`, acquires `threading.Lock()` (not `asyncio.Lock`), and calls `await payment_client.charge()`.
2. `payment_client.charge()` yields control back to the `asyncio` event loop while waiting on the TLS socket, with `threading.Lock` still held by the OS thread.
3. Request 2 arrives on the same event-loop thread, enters `checkout()`, and calls `lock.acquire()`.
4. Because `threading.Lock` is a blocking OS primitive already owned by the same thread (or waiting on Request 1's unlock), the event-loop thread immediately blocks inside the kernel `futex` syscall.
5. Even when Request 1's TLS socket receives the payment response 40 ms later, the event loop is frozen inside `futex` and can never poll Request 1 to reach `lock.release()`. Both requests—and every other connection on that worker—hang indefinitely.

sections.content:
## Runtimes and detection tools

Different runtimes expose distinct deadlock signatures and diagnostic tools:

- **Python (`asyncio`)**: Enable `PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1` or `loop.slow_callback_duration = 0.05` to flag callbacks blocking the loop >50 ms. Use `asyncio.to_thread()` for blocking libraries.
- **Rust (`tokio`)**: Run `tokio-console` to inspect task poll durations and waker counts, or enable `clippy::await_holding_lock` at compile time to catch `std::sync::Mutex` guards held across `.await`.
- **C# (.NET)**: Prefer `await` end-to-end; in libraries, use `.ConfigureAwait(false)` so continuations resume on the thread pool rather than a captured `SynchronizationContext`.
- **Java**: Avoid `ForkJoinPool.commonPool()` for blocking I/O; isolate blocking work to a dedicated `Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()` (Java 21+) or bounded `ThreadPoolExecutor`.

## Primitive comparison

| Primitive | Safe across `await`? | Overhead | Deadlock risk | Best use case |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `std::sync::Mutex` / `threading.Lock` | No | ~15–25 ns | High (self-deadlock / starvation) | Short in-memory critical sections with zero `.await` |
| `tokio::sync::Mutex` / `asyncio.Lock` | Yes | ~100–300 ns + waker | Low (lock-order only) | Guarding I/O resources or state across async steps |
| `Semaphore` (async) | Yes | ~100–250 ns | Low (permit exhaustion) | Bounding fan-out concurrency (e.g., max 32 DB calls) |
| Dedicated blocking pool | N/A (offloads) | ~5–20 µs thread hop | None on event loop | Legacy sync drivers, CPU-heavy hashing, file I/O |

## Failure modes

- **Silent pool starvation under load**: Code works in unit tests (1 request) and deadlocks in production (100 concurrent requests) when nested `.join()` calls exhaust all 8 worker threads.
- **Drop-after-partial-write corruption**: Cancelling a future via `tokio::select!` or `asyncio.wait_for()` mid-lock leaves shared state half-mutated unless operations are cancel-safe.
- **Re-entrant async lock deadlock**: Calling a helper that acquires the same non-reentrant `asyncio.Lock` within the same coroutine task hangs immediately.

## Structured concurrency & timeouts

Wrap every external `await` and lock acquisition in an explicit deadline (`asyncio.timeout(2.0)`, `tokio::time::timeout`) so a stalled dependency fails fast instead of pinning tasks indefinitely. Pair timeouts with structured task groups (`asyncio.TaskGroup` in Python 3.11+, `StructuredTaskScope` in Java) to guarantee child tasks are cancelled and joined before the parent scope exits, preventing orphaned background tasks from holding locks.

## Practical checklist

- Audit every async function for blocking calls (`sleep`, sync HTTP/DB drivers, `.Result`, `.get()`, `.join()`).
- Enable static lints (`clippy::await_holding_lock`) and debug loop monitors (`PYTHONASYNCIODEBUG=1`) in CI and staging.
- Drop synchronous mutex guards in an inner block before hitting any `.await`.
- Isolate unavoidable blocking calls onto a dedicated thread pool with bounded queue depth.
- Attach explicit timeouts to every lock acquisition and network `await`.

interviewProblems.title: Async/Await & Deadlock Avoidance
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Async/Await & Deadlock Avoidance. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Async/await turns non-blocking I/O into sequential-looking state machines, but mixing synchronous blocking calls, single-threaded event loops, or non-async-aware locks can freeze an entire runtime.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: I/O Driver (epoll) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Blocking Pool.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Blocking Pool experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Propagate `async`/`await` all the way to the entry point (`async all the way`), or use `ConfigureAwait(false)` in library code.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Never block an async worker thread waiting on a task that needs that same thread or executor to finish—use non-blocking awaits, async-aware locks, or dedicated blocking pools.
Avoid trap: Calling `time.sleep()`, `requests.get()`, or `psycopg2` inside a Python `async def` coroutine instead of `asyncio.sleep()`, `httpx.AsyncClient`, or `asyncpg`.
Avoid trap: Using `.Result` or `.get()` inside async callbacks as a quick bridge to synchronous interfaces.
When to reach for it: High-concurrency I/O-bound workloads (HTTP/gRPC gateways, database clients, fan-out aggregators) where threads spend >90% of time waiting on sockets.
When to reach for it: Structured concurrency trees where parent tasks spawn bounded child tasks and cancel them cleanly on timeout or error.

putItTogether.title: Putting Async Await Deadlocks Together
putItTogether.summary: Never block an async worker thread waiting on a task that needs that same thread or executor to finish—use non-blocking awaits, async-aware locks, or dedicated blocking pools.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Async Await Deadlocks before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: The HTTP call finishes on an I/O thread, but its continuation is posted back to the captured `SynchronizationContext`, which is permanently blocked inside `.Result`. Both threads wait forever.
